Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) is an acceleration structure for ray-primitive intersection that organizes scene primitives into a tree of nested bounding volumes to reduce the number of expensive primitive intersection tests [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim states that Hierarchical Bounding Volumes (HBV) is an acceleration structure for ray-primitive intersection that organizes scene primitives into a tree of nested bounding volumes to reduce the number of expensive primitive intersection tests. Source [S1] defines a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) as a tree where each node is associated with a subset of primitives and a bounding volume enclosing them, explicitly stating the basic idea is to 'save costs by precomputations... and filtering of the rays' (reducing intersection tests). Source [S2] describes 'Hierarchical Bounding Volumes' as a 'tree of bounding volumes where children are contained within their parent' used for 'acceleration' and provides an intersection algorithm that checks bounds before testing primitives. Both sources support the definition, structure (tree of nested volumes), and purpose (acceleration/reducing tests) described in the claim.

It solves the problem of linear search complexity in brute-force ray tracing by allowing rays to quickly discard large portions of the scene that do not intersect the current bounding volume [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the basic idea of Bounding Volumes (BVs) is to 'save costs by precomputations on the scene and filtering of the rays during run-time' and specifically notes that 'If the ray misses the BV, then it must also miss the enclosed object.' This confirms that rays can discard large portions of the scene (those enclosed by non-intersecting BVs). Furthermore, the evidence provides a table comparing 'Brute-force' rendering times against 'Goldsmith/Salmon BVH' times, showing significant performance gains (e.g., 24891.0 seconds vs 7.4 seconds for 66,430 spheres), which supports the claim that this method solves the problem of linear search complexity inherent in brute-force ray tracing.
